text:
When you type a web address, your browser has to turn that name into an IP address before it can load anything. That lookup is called DNS resolution, and DNS works a lot like the internet's address book.

The browser first checks its own cache, which holds addresses for sites you've visited recently. If the address isn't there, the request goes to a recursive resolver. The resolver asks a root server where to look next. The root server sends it to the right top-level domain server, such as the one for .com or .org. That server points it to the authoritative server, which has the actual address for the site.

The resolver sends that address back to your device, and the address gets cached. A value called the TTL (time to live) sets how long it stays cached, usually about 300 seconds. Until it expires, going back to the same site skips the lookup and loads faster. The whole process usually finishes in a fraction of a second.
